title: UODO (Poland) - DKE.561.5.2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
In September 2025, the DPA ordered the data controller to stop operating a video surveillance system which was covering his neighbours property and a public road. Additionally, he was required to erase the personal data of his neighbours (data subjects) from the recordings.
In December 2025 the data subject informed the DPA that the controller continued to use video surveillance extending beyond the boundaries of its property, thus failed to comply with the DPA’s order. The controller submitted a recording where neither the data subject’s property nor the public road was visible, and claimed that the video surveillance was exclusively for law enforcement purposes.
However, police records contradicted these claims by containing recordings of the controller, where the neighbours’ property and the public road were still visible. Additionally, the DPA found that the recording camera at the front of the house remained capable of being aimed at the subjects’ property until it was replaced with a fixed one in March 2026.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the controller breached it’s previous order by continuing to record the neighbour’s property and a public road after 16 October 2025. Compliance required a permanent technical solution preventing out-of-boundary surveillance. Occasional monitoring, live viewing, or assurance that cameras were aimed elsewhere were insufficient.
The controller’s security and evidence-gathering justification did not excuse non-compliance with the binding order. The DPA found full compliance only in March 2026, when the adjustable camera was replaced with a fixed one.
The DPA imposed a fine of PLN 1,470 (€335) under Article 83(6) GDPR, treating the breach as intentional but taking into account that the monitoring was not proven continuous and was eventually remedied.

title: HDPA (Greece) - Opinion 11/2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The Greek Ministry of Justice requested an opinion from the HDPA on a draft Ministerial Decision titled "Protocol of actions of forensic services in child abuse cases", issued under the enabling provision of Article 47(1)(a) of Law 5172/2025. Although framed as an internal protocol for forensic services, the draft introduced binding obligations for examining doctors across all public and private healthcare facilities in Greece, as well as for the Hellenic Police. Specifically, it mandated that attending physicians photograph "manifestly suspicious", "unusual”, or “suspicious" physical findings on minors during clinical examinations and forward these sensitive health records and images to criminal prosecution authorities. 
When the HDPA questioned whether the existing legislative delegation legally permitted imposing obligations on entities beyond forensic services, the Ministry pointed to a legislative amendment allowing joint decisions with co-competent Ministers. However, the text submitted to the HDPA remained formulated solely as a decision of the Minister of Justice. Consequently, the Authority assessed whether the proposed processing operations complied with the fundamental requirement of an adequate statutory legal basis under both EU data protection law and Greek constitutional requirements.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The HDPA issued a negative opinion on the draft decision, concluding as follows:
First and foremost, under Articles 6(1)(c)/(e), 6(3), and 9(2) GDPR, read in conjunction with Article 43(2) of the Greek Constitution, a Ministerial Decision cannot establish primary legal obligations or restrict rights for third parties -such as private physicians and clinics- without an adequately specific and clear legislative delegation, which the invoked provision lacked, as it covers the forensic medical service solely. 
Second, the draft violates data minimization under Article 5(1)(c) GDPR because it fails to restrict photography strictly to the necessary physical finding, thereby creating an unacceptable risk of capturing unaffected body parts or the minor's entire face. 
Third, the proposed framework fails to satisfy Articles 25 and 32 GDPR as it does not explicitly ban the use of doctors' personal mobile devices, misses requirements for dedicated authorized devices and immediate encrypted storage, lacks cryptographic hashing to guarantee evidentiary integrity, and permits printed paper circulations that increase data leakage risks. 
Fourth, pursuant to Article 35 GDPR, a formal Data Protection Impact Assessment is strictly mandatory before implementation, given that the processing involves the systematic handling of special categories of data of vulnerable data subjects.

title: Rb. Midden-Nederland - C/16/608667 / HA RK 26-54
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The data subject was involved in disputes with a school organisation ("controller"). Those disputes concerned a communication ban, their membership in a participation council, and their internship. 
The data subject submitted an access request under Article 15 GDPR. The controller provided an overview of the personal data it processed, but the data subject considered the controller's response incomplete. They argued that further access was necessary to verify the accuracy and completeness of their personal data. 
Consequently, the data subject initiated proceedings and requested the Court to order the controller to provide:
a. Complete copies of specific internal and external emails relating to the data subject; and 
b. The underlying transmission metadata to verify the accuracy of the information. 


Holding[edit | edit source]
The Court recognised that providing an overview of the personal data processed might be sufficient to comply with an access request under Article 15 GDPR. However it added that the underlying copies and transcripts might also fall within the scope of Article 15 if they are indispensable for the data subject to effectively exercise their rights under the GDPR.
The Court found the data subject's reasoning sufficient and ordered the controller to provide the requested documents. It confirmed that the accuracy and completeness of the personal data contained could only be determined by reading the full content of those documents. 
However, the Court rejected the request for transmission metadata. It considered this as falling outside the scope of Article 15 GDPR. Furthermore, the Court found no evidence to assume that the controller deliberately altered or withheld information that would require an analysis of the metadata.
Lastly, the Court also held that the personal data of the third parties should be appropriately anonymised and redacted when providing the documents.
The Court ordered the controller to provide the requested personal data within 14 days, subject to a penalty payment of € 250 per day for each day of non-compliance, with a maximum of € 25,000.

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali (Italy) - 759/2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received two complaints by Chiara Poggi’s parents regarding the publication in a news article by Cairo Editore (the controller) of images of the Garlasco murder of 2007. The article concerned the reopening of the investigation of a well-known murder and corresponding significant public interest. The images depicted Chiara Poggi’s body on the stairs at the crime scene surrounded by bloodstains, her face was blurred however the rest of her body visible.
The parent’s argued that publication of such images causes immense distress, infringed upon the dignity and memory of the victim and the interests and rights of the parents to protect her dignity and memory. Essentially, the parents argued that the inclusion of the images were unnecessary for the purposes of journalistic reporting of the murder.
The controller argued the freedom of expression, right to report the news and the public interest which had reignited as a result of the reopening of the investigation.  Particularly, the controller made emphasis of the fact that the image was included to help readers envision the crime scene and thus relevant to the article, clarifying that the disturbing nature of the image did not automatically make it an unlawful publication. The controller held that it acted in good faith, adopted safeguards to protect privacy, and implemented organisational measures.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA assessed whether the publishing by the controller, of these images of the Garlasco murder was necessary and proportionate.
The DPA found that in light of the well-known nature of this murder, the crime scene and circumstances had already been reported about multiple times. In this regard, the DPA considered that the addition of the images in the article did not add meaningful information which helped contribute to readers understanding the facts of the case.
Similarly, the DPA acknowledged the blurring out of the face, however found that, even if partially obscured, the exposure of the victim’s body and the bloodstains, resulted in a harm to her dignity.
Finally, the DPA understood the renewed public interest in the matter however did not find this a sufficient justification to publish the images. The DPA found that the controller was able to depict the reopening of the case, and heightened public interest without including the images. This resulted in the DPA deciding that the intrusion into the victim’s dignity and memory was disproportionate to the contribution of these images to public interest and understanding of the case.
In light of the foregoing, the DPA declared the publishing by the controller of these images as unlawful in accordance to Articles 5(1)(a) and (c), and Article 85 GDPR as well as the Italian Privacy Code and Journalistic Ethics Rules. The DPA did not issue a fine however pursuant to Article 58(2)(f) GDPR prohibited further dissemination of these images.

title: Tietosuojavaltuutetun toimisto (Finland) - TSV/5175/2025
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A customer (the data subject) had undergone laser tattoo removal at a plastic surgery clinic (the controller). The data subject had repeatedly requested access to their patient records between 2016 and 2025, which had remained unanswered. The Consumer Disputes Board had issued a decision in 2023 where it recommended that the controller pay the data subject compensation for errors that occurred during the laser tattoo removal procedure. 
The data subject lodged a complaint with the DPA in May 2025 regarding the failure to reply to the access requests. The controller argued that it did not offer laser tattoo removals and claimed that the data subject had never been its customer. 
The DPA issued a decision on 29 June 2026 and ordered the controller to provide the data subject access to their personal data under Articles 15(1) and (3) GDPR no later than 29 August 2026. The data subject notified the DPA that they had not received this information on 30 August. Following this, the DPA initiated the present proceedings to investigate whether the controller had complied with the order. 
The controller reported on 4 October 2026 that it had found information pertaining to the data subject. The data subject stated that this data consisted solely of the company’s own notes and only contained the date and cost of the appointment instead of official patient records.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the controller had failed to comply with its order to provide the data subject access to the information required under Articles 15(1) and (3) GDPR by 29 June 2026. It issued the controller a fine of €20,200.
The DPA pointed out that the controller had not fulfilled the data subject's access request on 4 October either: the information sent to the data subject did not include all details required under the Finnish Client Data Act (703/2023). Furthermore, the controller's claim of not offering laser tattoo removals was disproven by the decision of the Consumer Disputes Board from 2023 as well as information on the controller's website stating the contrary. Even if the controller had provided the requested information in October, the deadline set in the DPA's previous decision had already been exceeded.

title: DVI (Latvia) - SIA "K4K"
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA initiated an investigation into the processing of personal data on the website of a company operating fitness clubs (the controller) in October 2025. The DPA then ordered the controller to take additional steps to ensure that its processing of personal data would comply with the GDPR and the national data protection provisions. 
In December 2025, the DPA sent the controller a letter by email requesting the controller to report the corrections made. As no response was received by the specified deadline, the DPA repeated the request and set a new deadline in January 2026. This email also remained unanswered. In March 2026, the DPA sent the letter to the controller's legal address by mail. This letter was returned to the DPA with a note from the postal service provider stating that the retention period for the letter had expired.
Following the controller's failure to respond, the DPA initiated administrative proceedings for the imposition of a fine under Articles 58(2)(i) and 83(5)(e) GDPR. It notified the controller of the date and time of a hearing in this case in July 2026. The controller neither replied nor appeared at the hearing. 


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA imposed a fine of €500 on the controller for a failure to provide the requested information on the corrections implemented on the controller's website. Therefore, it held that the controller had violated Article 58(1)(e). 
The DPA pointed out that the controller is obliged to cooperate with the DPA upon request pursuant to Article 31 GDPR. When calculating the amount of the fine, the DPA took into account that the violation was ongoing and had not ceased. The controller had also not cooperated with the DPA. On the other hand, the controller had not previously infringed the GDPR. All in all, the DPA found the violation at issue to be minor.

title: BVwG - W101 2326836-1
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
40 natural persons submitted access requests to a mobile communications provider (controller) via an attorney. Some of these persons were (former) customers of the controller, others have never been in a contractual relationship with the controller.
In the access requests, the data subjects requested access to information regarding a service fee that the data subjects are supposed to have paid to the controller on an annual basis in the past. A court has decided that this service fee was unlawful. Consequently, customers could claim to be refunded.
The attorney advertised on his website to aid data subjects with claiming the refund of the service fee, and that evidence for the procedure to claim the refund could be obtained with an access request under Article 15 GDPR.
The access request that the attorney submitted to the controller contained the name and date of birth of the data subjects and their ID. The attorney referred to a power of attorney, however it was not attached. 
The controller did not reply to the requests. Consequently, the data subjects lodged a complaint with the DPA. The DPA decided that the controller violated Article 15 GDPR by not responding to the request. The controller appealed the DPA’s decision to the Federal Administrative Court (Bundesverwaltungsgericht).

Holding[edit | edit source]
As far as the access requests of the non-costumers were concerned, the court held that the controller violated Article 15 GDPR. 
Despite the fact that the mobile communications provider did not process any personal data about the non-customers, in a case such as the one at hand, Article 15(1) GDPR provides that the  de facto controller is obliged to confirm that they do not process any personal data. The person has a reasonable interest to know whether or not personal data about them is being processed.
The requests could not be denied on the basis of Article 12(6) GDPR on the grounds of reasonable doubts concerning the identity of the person making the request since the attorney did not provide their power of attorney. There is no general obligation of the person who made the access request to provide additional information, only when there are reasonable doubts concerning their identity. The same must be true for the provision of a power of attorney. 
There is no provision in the GDPR or national law that prohibits an attorney from filing an access request for a natural person. According to the court, there were no reasonable doubts concerning the lawful representation by the attorney because it does not seem likely that the attorney had unlawfully obtained and used copies of the IDs of several persons, and provided their name and birth date in order to file access requests. Article 12(6) GDPR was not applicable.
The access requests were not excessive pursuant to Article 12(5) GDPR because no abusive exercise was found. Because the non-customers never paid the service fee, their access request cannot be rejected as excessive on the grounds that they pursued extraneous purposes in the form of preparation of civil-law claims.
As far as the access requests of the (former) customers were concerned, the court found no violation of Article 15 GDPR.  
According to the court, the controller could rely on Article 12(5) GDPR. The access requests of the (former) customers were excessive because they were not based on data protection related reasons. The court was convinced that, if it was not for the service fee, the data subjects would not have had any interest in access to their personal information processed by the controller. According to CJEU case law, already the first access request of a data subject to a controller can be excessive. 
The data subjects’ objective was to claim the refund of the service fee. The court inferred this from the fact that the attorney actively promoted such a practice on their website. Moreover, there are 1,000 similar court cases pending where data subjects requested access to their personal data in relation to a service fee of a mobile communications provider since a court has found the service fees were unlawful.

title: CJEU - C-222/25 - Rahapesu Andmebüroo
text:
Contents

1 English Summary

1.1 Facts
1.2 Advocate General Opinion
1.3 Holding





English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The data subject made an access request to the Rahapesu Andmebüroo (Financial Intelligence Unit of Estonia, and controller). The data subject sought to determine whether information concerning him had been transmitted to, or whether enquiries had been made by, Estonian or foreign credit institutions or foreign authorities. Two separate requests.
The controller rejected the data subject’s access requests on the basis of the national law on the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing and the law on public information. Particularly, as these laws prevented the controller from disclosing data collected in the course of its duties or any information regarding the existence or exchange of such data.
The data subject brought the matter before the Administrative Court, and the Court of Appeal which dismissed the proceedings. The Supreme Court of Estonia however set aside the preceding judgments and ordered the controller to issue a new decision on the data subject’s access requests. Specifically, the Supreme Court held that in the absence of criminal proceedings the GDPR is applicable to the right of access by the data subject to his personal data. Additionally, it was emphasised that the referenced national law automatically restricts data subject’s access right but rather confers the power, onto the controller’s foreman, to restrict access by classifying the information as intended for internal use only. Nonetheless, this was not the case.
In the meantime, prior to the conclusion of the above proceedings, the data subject submitted a third request, asking whether an investigation file had been opened on him and whether inquiries were made to the United States of America. This request was once again rejected by the controller. 
The data subject then submitted a complaint to the DPA which upheld the decision and ordered the controller to re-examine the request for information. The controller rejected and relied on national law to underscore its obligation to preserve the confidentiality of the information contained in their database to protect the Estonian financial system. 
The data subject challenged the decisions of the controller before the Administrative Court who ruled in the data subject’s favour that national law was incompatible with Article 23 GDPR. This was especially because the national law was insufficiently clear and precise and did not give grounds to restrict access or the duration of such restrictions. The controller appealed this decision to the Tallin Court of Appeal, nonetheless it was dismissed.
The Court of Appeal upheld the Administrative Courts decision and added that the decision by the controller imposed an absolute and unlimited restriction to the right of access which was disproportionate.
The controller appealed to the Estonian Supreme Court which turned to the CJEU for a preliminary ruling on four questions.  

Primarily, whether the personal data processing by an FIU constitutes processing by a competent authority for purposes of the Law Enforcement Directive (LED) even if it is not an investigative body?
Secondly, whether in administrative or judicial proceedings it is possible to refuse an access request without a legal basis to avoid confirming or denying their processing, and denying information about the data subject’s right to judicial review under the LED?
Thirdly, whether national law which permits an FIU head to restrict data subject’s rights with the purpose, conditions and temporal and geographical scope specified across multiple legal provisions?
Fourthly, whether the provisions of the LED and GDPR are to be interpreted as permitting national legislation to restrict access to personal data until their deletion (storage limitation), permanently preventing data subjects from obtaining information about their data?
Advocate General Opinion[edit | edit source]
1. Applicability of the GDPR to FIUs
In light of the courts case law, the core mission, function and role of the controller and other FIU’s, the Advocate General opined that data processing by the controller for the purposes of crime prevention in the field of Anti-money Laundering or Combating the Financing of Terrorism falls within the scope of the LED. Irrespective of the controller’s status or lack of status as an investigative body under national procedural law.  Nonetheless, where the controller processes data for purposes which are unrelated to its core mission in the field of Anti-money Laundering or Combating the Financing of Terrorism, such processing falls within the scope of the GDPR.
In this regard, if the controller (an FIU) is competent to take autonomous decisions to analyse, request and disseminate financial intelligence information, and has significant powers conferred by EU law necessary for crime detection and prevention in the field of Anti-money Laundering or Combating the Financing of Terrorism such processing falls within the scope of the LED. 
2. Data Subject’s Right of Access under Article 15 LED 
The Advocate General opined that the right of access under Article 15 LED allows for Member States to adopt national law which completely restricts data subject’s right to access to data held by an FIU. This is especially so where such is necessary to protect the effectiveness and confidentiality of the anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing system.
The Advocate General clarified that this is permitted insofar as the national law laying down such a rule is sufficiently clear and precise as to the scope and application of the measure. Additionally, it must be accompanied by minimum safeguards which allow data subjects to be provided with sufficient guarantees that such data will be effectively protected against the risk of abuse and unlawful access or use by an FIU. Furthermore, such laws must ensure data subjects are allowed to have refusals reviewed by supervisory authorities and courts, and provide for the indirect exercise of their rights under Article 17 LED.
Ultimately, the Advocate General stated that EU law precludes a complete access right restriction which lasts until the storage limitation and subsequent deletion of the data where the above requirements are not satisfied. 
3. Refusal of access without disclosing the legal base 
The Advocate General emphasised that under Article 15(3) LED where a restriction to the right of access applies, the data subject must be informed of the restriction and reasons for such, without undue delay. Nonetheless, this information may be omitted where it would undermine a purpose of public interest. Therefore, the Advocate General held that this allows the controller to provide a response such as to neither confirm or deny, omitting information as to whether personal data processing was being carried out at all. 
Nonetheless, the Advocate General highlighted that this must be followed by informing data subjects of the possibility to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority or to seek judicial remedy pursuant to Article 15(3) LED. Additionally, in accordance with Article 17(2) LED, where direct access is denied, the controller is obliged to inform the data subject of the possibility of exercising their rights indirectly through the supervisory authority. The Advocate General clarified that whilst the reasons to refuse access may be withheld from data subjects, the controller retains the obligation to document such reasons and make such information available to the supervisory authorities (Article 15(4) LED).
4. LED precluding national legislation permitting the restriction of right of access  
The Advocate General highlighted that, pursuant to Article 15(1) LED, any restriction of the right of access by data subjects requires the adoption of legislative measures by Member States, and is to be understood broadly. This is so that it is not only satisfied there a single legislative act which governs all aspects of the restriction of access but also by a set of legislative provisions. However, the Advocate General clarified that when referencing such a legislative measure, it must be clear and precise, allowing data subjects to be able to identify the circumstances and conditions under which the scope of the rights conferred on them by the LED may be applicable and restricted. 
In the present case, the Advocate General identified a number of provisions relevant to the right of access by the controller. However also stressed the general nature of the provisions did not allow the data subject to understand the specific circumstances and conditions of the restriction and the safeguards implemented against the risk of abuse.
5. Conclusion
The Advocate General opined the processing of personal data by an FIU such as the controller, falls within the scope of the LED notwithstanding its classification under national criminal procedural law. Whilst restrictions on the right of access by data subjects may be justified in light of protecting investigations and preventing disclosure of sensitive information, such a restriction must be governed by clear and precise rules and be accompanied by adequate safeguards against abuse. Where an FIU may withhold the reasons to refuse access, data subjects must be informed of their right to seek access through the supervisory authority.

Holding[edit | edit source]
tbd

title: CJEU - C‑568/25 - Universal Versand
text:
Contents

1 English Summary

1.1 Facts
1.2 Advocate General Opinion

1.2.1 1. Legal effect on data subjects or similarly significantly affect them
1.2.2 2. The notion of “necessity” pursuant to Article 22(2)(a) GDPR, categories of data, and burden of proof
1.2.3 a. Notion of “necessity”
1.2.4 b. Categories of data and burden of proof
1.2.5 3. Interpretation of “decision” under Article 22(2) GDPR
1.2.6 4. Conclusion


1.3 Holding





English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The controller is a mail order business that handles several ten thousand monthly orders. It offers its customers the option to pay in instalments or payment on open account. Those payment methods amount to 90% of all payments. Before a customer is offered one of these payment methods, the controller is conducting an internal credit assessment for existing customers and a credit assessment via a credit information agency for new customers. In case of a negative result, the payment method is denied. 
There are alternative payment methods available to all customers regardless of a credit assessment (payment via credit card or PayPal).
An organisation launched a class action against this procedure with the Regional Court Linz (Landgericht Linz). The Regional Court dismissed the class action. The organisation unsuccessfully appealed the decision to the Higher Regional Court Linz (Oberlandesgericht Linz). The organisation further appealed the decision to the Higher Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) that referred to the CJEU the question for a preliminary ruling whether the above-mentioned procedure produces a legal effect concerning the customers or similarly significantly affects them (Article 22(1) GDPR). Moreover, the referring court asks for the interpretation of the criterium of “necessity” pursuant to Article 22(2)(a) GDPR, and whether only personal data that is necessary for the performance of a contract can be processed for the automated decision-making and where the burden of proof for the notion of necessity lies. Finally, the referring court asks whether the word “decision” in Article 22(2) GDPR must be interpreted as “automated decision”.

Advocate General Opinion[edit | edit source]
1. Legal effect on data subjects or similarly significantly affect them[edit | edit source]
According to Advocate General Medina (AG), the denial of a payment method on the basis of an automated decision has a legal effect on the data subject or similarly significantly affects them, when the decision prevents the data subject from entering into a contract. The criterium of “legal effect” requires that the decision can affect the character or exercise of a person’s rights and obligations. As far as the criterium of “similarly significantly affect” is concerned, the decision must have an objective and significant impact on the data subject, and not only hypothetically or marginally affect them. Moreover, the effect on the data subject must be of comparable quality to a legal effect.
The AG referred to the jurisprudence of the CJEU (C 634/21 SCHUFA Holding u.a. (Scoring)) that held that a decision similarly significantly affected a data subject when the result of an automated credit assessment almost systematically led to the rejection of a credit application by a consumer. A consumer credit can be comparable to a purchase with instalments or payment on open account. Therefore, both cases must be treated identically (comparability of the character of the payment method with a consumer credit).
Additionally, the exclusion of a payment method where the customer is allowed to pay at least a certain amount after the conclusion of the contract can lead to a customer’s inability to make a purchase. In this regard, when it comes to the effect of the automated decision, namely the inability to conclude a contract, the case at hand and the quoted CJEU case (rejection of a consumer credit because of a negative credit assessment) are comparable as well. 
The decision to exclude a payment method for a customer that is based solely on automated decision-making of the payment default probability has a legal effect or similarly significantly affects the customer when it is likely to prevent the conclusion of the contract, according to the AG.

2. The notion of “necessity” pursuant to Article 22(2)(a) GDPR, categories of data, and burden of proof[edit | edit source]
a. Notion of “necessity”[edit | edit source]
As far as the notion of “necessity” pursuant to Article 22(2)(a) GDPR is concerned, the AG draws a parallel to the interpretation of “necessity” pursuant to Article 6(1)(b) GDPR. According to CJEU case law, the processing is necessary for the performance of a contract pursuant to Article 6(1)(b) GDPR when the main subject matter of the contract cannot be achieved if the processing in question does not occur, and there are no workable, less intrusive alternatives. 
The decision is necessary for entering into, or performance of, a contract when there is an objective link between the decision (automated creditworthiness assessment with the purpose of determining a suitable payment method) and the achievement of the main subject matter of the contract (purchase of goods). Moreover, there shall be no workable, less intrusive means. 
According to the AG, it is possible that the automated decision-making serves the purpose of achieving the main subject matter of the contract. In order to assess that question it is necessary to determine whether the purpose of offering a suitable payment method serves the achievement of the main subject matter of the contract. Additionally, it must be determined whether the question of suitability of payment methods depends on the outcome of the creditworthiness assessment via automated decision-making. This assessment shall not be achieved by workable, less intrusive means.  
If the question is answered in the affirmative, the assessment is necessary for achieving the main subject matter of the contract. This is for the referring court to determine. The same is true for the question whether the automated processing is a suitable means to achieve that purpose. 

b. Categories of data and burden of proof[edit | edit source]
The referring court asks whether the data processed for automated decision-making must be objectively necessary for the performance of a contract. According to the AG, when it comes to the quantitative assessment of the personal data that is necessary, the data minimisation principle must be considered pursuant to Article 5 GDPR. Therefore, only the data that is necessary for the purpose of processing can lawfully be processed. It is for the referring court to decide whether the processed data is necessary for the credit assessment. In order to make the assessment what factors are relevant for the credit assessment, the court shall take into consideration national law concerning the purpose of the contract and consumer protection.
Additionally, the referring court asks whether the burden of proof as to the necessity of processing of data for the performance of a contract lies with the controller or the data subject. The AG referred to Article 5(2) GDPR that stipulates that the controller shall bear the burden of proof of compliance with the principles of processing pursuant to Article 5(1) GDPR. According to the AG, the burden of proof to demonstrate that the main subject matter of the contract cannot be achieved without the processing in the context of Article 22(2)(a) GDPR lies with the controller. This is because of the similarity to Article 6(1)(b) GDPR, where the CJEU has already decided that the burden of proof lies with the controller that allows for a parallel to be drawn to Article 22(2)(a) GDPR.

3. Interpretation of “decision” under Article 22(2) GDPR[edit | edit source]
According to the AG, the “decision” that Article 22(2) refers to is to be read as an “automated decision” and not just any “decision”. Therefore, Article 22(2)(a) GDPR is applicable only when the automated decision is necessary for entering into, or performance of a contract. 
It is not enough for the controller to demonstrate that the automation of the decision is beneficial. It must be the only option in order to achieve the performance of the contract. A human shall not be capable of making that decision for practical reasons such as the amount of data to be processed. It is for the controller to prove that the number of orders and the speed with which the decisions about the availability of payment methods must be made require automated decision-making as the only feasible option, as opposed to a less intrusive method. Moreover, the controller must demonstrate that a prompt decision about the payment method offered is a decisive factor for the customer to enter into the contract. 

4. Conclusion[edit | edit source]
According to the AG, a decision on a creditworthiness assessment that can lead to the exclusion of payment methods has a legal effect on a data subject or similarly significantly affects them when the decision can prevent the conclusion of a contract. Article 22(2)(a) GDPR is applicable when there is an objective link between the subject matter of the contract and the automated decision-making on the credit assessment. The processed data must be necessary for making that decision, which is for the controller to prove. Finally, the notion of “decision” pursuant to Article 22(2) GDPR must be understood as “automated decision”.


Holding[edit | edit source]
tbd

title: OLG Hamm - 22 U 77/25
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The data subject had been using a social media platform operated by the controller since September 2020 for exclusively private purposes. The data subject opposed the collection and processing of personal data generated when visiting third-party websites using the controller’s so-called “Business Tools” in a manner that could be linked to him and his profile on the controller’s platform. Implementing these business tools involved transmitting data to third-party websites in order to display targeted advertising to the user.
The data subject filed a lawsuit seeking a declaratory judgment stating that the processing was unlawful. In addition, the data subject sought a cease and desist order, restriction of processing, erasure, and compensation for non-pecuniary damages. The court dismissed the data subject’s action as partially inadmissible and partially unfounded in May 2025. The data subject appealed this decision to the Higher Regional Court Hamm.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The court held that the data subject’s claims were well-founded. First, it concluded that the processing of personal data in connection with the business tools had been unlawful. Second, the court ordered the controller to refrain from processing personal data on third-party websites and apps outside the controller's networks, to restrict the processing of the unlawfully processed data, and to erase all of this data that already been stored one month after the final and binding conclusion of the proceedings. Third, the court granted the data subject €750 in non-pecuniary damages for the loss of control over their personal data.
The court held that the defendant had violated Article 6(1) GDPR and the principle of lawfulness laid down in Article 5(1)(a) GDPR, as it lacked a legal basis for the processing. According to the court, the controller had obtained consent solely for the purpose of providing personalised advertising and therefore could not invoke Article 6(1)(a) GDPR to process data for security and integrity purposes. Furthermore, the court held that the data subject had implicitly revoked their consent within the meaning of Article 7(3) GDPR by filing a complaint against the controller. 
The controller could not rely on the other legal bases in Articles 6(1)(b)–(e) GDPR either, as there was no evidence that the requirements for these legal bases were met. In particular, the processing was not necessary for the performance of the contract between the controller and the data subject. Moreover, the controller had not even invoked the existence of legitimate interests against the data subject.
In addition, the controller had violated the principle of transparency set forth in Article 5(1)(a) GDPR. The court pointed out that the functioning and impact of the business tools constituted a technically complex matter. An average user could not be expected to understand how their data are processed based on the controller’s approximately 150-page privacy notice.
Finally, the court found that the controller had not specified the purposes and the extent of processing through its business tools sufficiently clearly. The controller had therefore also violated the principles of purpose limitation and data minimisation laid down in Articles 5(1)(b) and 5(1)(c) GDPR respectively.

title: ANSPDCP (Romania) - Fine against MYCONNECTOR PLATFORM S.R.L
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
MyConnector Platform SRL (the controller) used real personal data in a testing environment while developing and testing its application. In this context, a cyberattack that targeted the controller’s testing server allowed an unauthorised third party to access that personal data, including contact and identification details of users.
Following the incident, the controller notified the Romanian DPA of the personal data breach under Article 33 GDPR, which led the authority to launch an investigation.


Holding[edit | edit source]
First, the Romanian DPA found that the controller infringed Article 32(1)(b) GDPR and Article 32(2) GDPR by failing to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the confidentiality and integrity of personal data processed in its testing environment. This violation allowed a cyberattack on the controller's test server, resulting in unauthorised access to personal data.
Second, the Romanian DPA considered it particularly relevant that the controller used real personal data, rather than fictitious data, in its development and testing environment. According to the authority, this practice increased the impact of the incident because it exposed the personal data of a significant number of data subjects when the testing server was compromised. 
The DPA therefore concluded that the controller had failed to ensure the confidentiality and integrity of its processing systems and services, in breach of Article 32 GDPR. It imposed a fine of €6,000 (RON 31,451) and ordered the implementation of an internal procedure requiring the exclusive use of fictitious data in development and testing environments, as a corrective measure.
